hits.full_text:
Has anyone else been yanked around by @DNAComplete? 

Sent them samples for a family member more than a year ago with payment. No results to date, just "Your results are being processed" 

When I emailed DNAComplete, their response was effectively "We never promised any timeline for results" (see pasted portion below). Something doesn't add up. 

Multiple follow ups have led to "You should have results in 6-8 weeks." That comes and goes, and I get another similar message. Customer service seems to have a playbook for this scenario, so it's hard to imagine I'm the only case. 

Anyone else had issues, or did I just pull the joker card?

I mean, I've heard of companies getting into trouble for boosting revenue something like this: customers pay for premium product and wait, company books revenue, chargeback period expires or is pegged to "expected delivery date," company says there was *never* an expected delivery date, 99.9% of customers dealing with non-delivery of product give up.

Here's an excerpt from their first email response:

"Thank you for following up with the DNA Complete support team.

We understand your concerns and recognize that the extended processing time can be difficult, and we appreciate your continued patience. As a reminder, DNA Complete does not guarantee turnaround times for sequencing and reporting due to the variables involved in laboratory processing."

I ran through their checkout process again and couldn't find any mention of "does not guarantee turnaround times." Maybe it's fine print. If they change the website after this tweet, look at Wayback Machine.

Lab processing? More than a year? C'mon, now. I've worked with labs over decades, and I call BS. Even if you're running the sample now, is it even intact 12+ months later?

Best case, my guess is that they lost track of the sample or lost it entirely. Worst case? Who knows, but I'm not buying the lab processing and repeated brush offs.

It's very rare that I post stuff like this, but the vast majority of people would have no recourse if caught in this situation. So I wanted to see if it's a wider problem the company needs to address. Maybe it can save other people headaches and money.
hits.hook: Ferriss: complaint thread about a DNA testing company; low fit
hits.draft_en:
If I picture still doing this in five years, I make different choices today. Fewer products. Slower writing. A notebook I'll actually finish.

The long version of a thing is almost always quieter than the short one.

hits.full_text:
Long-term thinking changes your short-term actions.

-When you intend to invest long-term, it changes which stocks you buy.
-When you intend to be in a relationship long-term, it changes the type of person you look for.
-When you intend to stay injury-free for the long term, it changes the type of workouts you do.

Build what lasts.

patterns: Boring basics win: Bloom's 'I regret to inform you that a lot of problems in life are solved by waking up early and working out' (~103k, 517 saves). The 'I regret to inform you' opener makes a plain truth feel like a confession. Brand angle: the boring fix, done again tomorrow.

Long view: Clear's 'Long-term thinking changes your short-term actions' (~68.8k, 790 saves) uses a three-line 'When you intend to... it changes...' list and a short closer. Outsiders echo it ('changes what short-term setbacks mean'), and crypto bots spam the phrase, so don't reuse it word for word.

Invitation hooks: Clear's 'What is a beautiful quote or passage about the natural world?' (~17.6k, 38 replies) asks the audience to bring something. Good, warm reply territory, and it rewards a real, accurate quote.
Honesty over flattery: Ferriss's 'Most people want to tell you what you want to hear' (~7k, fresh). Pairs with the brand's honest, dry tone.
Skip: Ferriss's DNAComplete complaint thread (~90.5k) is a grievance post. High views, wrong energy for the brand, and no reply.

Outsiders: fountain pens are everywhere, from first-pen posts ('omg. i get it.') to collector jokes and a 'fountain pen era over' post about upkeep. 'AI is pushing me to analog' and 'typing is faster, writing sticks better' are the quieter, more on-brand threads. 'Tiny habits, big glow-up' is wellness-saturated; avoid it.
Still climbing: Bloom's 'outlast uncertainty' went from ~6.9k at yesterday's run to ~131.4k (1,013 saves). Clear's 'use what you already know' is ~55.1k and Ferriss's 'critical few' is ~53k.

reply_ideas.reply_text: Rachel Carson, in The Sense of Wonder: "Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts." It's a short book and worth reading in one sitting.
Annoyingly true. The part people skip is making it small enough to keep. A walk counts on the bad days. The version you'll still be doing in February is the one that actually solves things.
Which is why the people who tell you the slightly uncomfortable thing, kindly, are worth keeping close. They're rarer than good advice.
